headlines.title: California lawmaker Aisha Wahab wins special election to succeed Eric Swalwell in Congress
headlines.description: What to Know State Sen. Aisha Wahab has won a special election for California’s Congressional District 14, NBC News projects. The Congressional District 14 seat was vacated earlier this year when former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell resigned from Congress after sexual assault and misconduct allegations. Wahab will fill Swalwell’s seat through January. At that time, the winner of the regular general election in November will take over for a full, two-year term. California’s 14th Congressional District includes the East Bay cities such as Fremont, Hayward and Livermore. California lawmaker Aisha Wahab secured victory Thursday in a special election to serve the rest of former Rep. Eric Swalwell’s House term, which ends in January. Swalwell, a Democrat who was running for California governor, ended his campaign and resigned from Congress in April after he was accused of sexual assault and harassment. He has denied the allegations. Wahab defeated Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez in the special election in the state’s 14th Congressional District, which covers parts of Alameda County on the eastern side of the San Francisco Bay. Wahab has championed housing affordability and access. She also wrote a bill in 2023 to ban caste-based discrimination, which garnered national attention. Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed it, saying such discrimination is already outlawed by civil rights protections. Wahab became the first Afghan American elected to public office in the U.S. when she won a Hayward City Council seat in 2018. She’ll be the first Afghan American to serve in Congress. The conclusion of the race to replace Swalwell comes as criminal investigations continue into the sexual assault allegations he faces. Over the weekend, federal agents seized electronic devices from Swalwell at the San Francisco airport and later searched his home in Washington D.C., according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to publicly discuss an ongoing investigation and spoke on the condition of anonymity. California 20 hours ago Decision 2026 Aug 18 Swalwell’s attorney did not immediately respond to an email and phone message seeking comment. Wahab and Hernandez will face off again in a separate November election determining who will serve the next full two-year term. Wahab won the June primary decisively, but she’s been up against a swell of spending boosting her rival ahead of the general. Groups affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, poured millions into supporting Hernandez, and thousands into opposing Wahab. Hernandez issued the following statement Thursday after the race was called: “I’ve been a fighter my whole life, and when I promised the residents of CA-14 I would fight for them, I never gave up. In just 63 days, we closed a gap from 26,000 votes to 6,000 votes by sharing our message of lowering housing costs, creating jobs, and supporting strong public safety. Voters finally got the chance to see what I have been doing as a mom, Dublin’s Mayor, and a director of healthcare services. The election for CA-14 in November will be in the new district lines, adding 26,000 Dublin voters who didn’t have the chance to vote for me in August. We’re looking forward to winning this on November 3rd with a more favorable district and a much larger electorate. Game on!” Associated Press reporter Alanna Drukin Richer contributed from Washington.

headlines.title: Proposed indoor shooting range in Walnut Creek sparks debate
headlines.description: A proposal to transform a vacant commercial building into a nine-lane shooting range in Walnut Creek has drawn mixed reaction for people living nearby. The proposal from Elite Armory would transform a former carpet store on North Main Street into a nine-lane indoor shooting range with firearms training, instructional classes and retail sales. The company also wants to expand the existing building, add parking and make other exterior improvements. The building is located in a commercial area surrounded by businesses like car dealerships and auto service shops. Serge has lived in Walnut Creek for years and as someone who goes to shooting ranges, he says he’d welcome one closer to home. “Honestly speaking, I’m fine with it. We don’t have many shooting ranges here,” he said. But opposition also emerged during Wednesday’s Design Review Commission meeting, with some questioning whether a shooting range belongs in this part of the city. Those who spoke at the meeting say the area is also close to homes and families, and question whether a gun range fits the character of the neighborhood. Elite Armory’s Co-Owner Gabriel Casillas says safety is at the center of the design. “Thank you for the option to speak today and give some more background on our business,” Casillas said. The proposed range would have a ballistic ceiling,impact-resistant walls and sound-absorbing materials. The company also presented a noise study saying the range would not have a significant impact on the surrounding area. The debate isn’t one-sided; the city says it received 101 emails about the proposal with 54% opposed and 44% in support. The city says it wants residents to stay involved as the project moves through the review process. “We encourage residents and other interested parties to continue participating in the public review process as the application moves through the public review process,” the city said in a statement. For some residents, support or opposition may ultimately come down to how the range would operate. “If it’s done right, it’s fine. Just like anything else, there has to be risk management, and you have to be aware of the surroundings you know,” Walnut Creek resident Orbie Diaz Said. The Design Review Commission will make a recommendation on the project, but it will not make the final decision. The next major step will be a hearing before the Walnut Creek Planning Commission where the conditional use permit will be considered. That meeting has not yet been scheduled. Any decision there could later be appealed to the City Council.

headlines.title: Coastal farmworkers feel the squeeze: ‘The money coming in just isn't enough'
headlines.description: Working full-time picking strawberries and watering trees for minimum wage wasn’t enough to put food on his family’s table, so Pescadero farmworker Margarito Gomez said he decided to grow his own. “The word minimum says it all,” said Gomez, a husband and father of four who moved to the area 25 years ago. “It’s the minimum to survive.” When Gomez wraps up his day job every afternoon, he heads over to Gavilanes Farm, the farm he owns and operates with friends on land they lease from a neighbor. The farm – which mostly grows beans and tomatoes – helps guarantee his family will have healthy food to eat. “We’re taking it very seriously,” he said. “Right now we’re farming four acres.” But so far, the farm isn’t making a profit and Gomez said he also does maintenance work for his landlord in exchange for a discount on the rent. He’s not the only one feeling the squeeze. The coastal towns that house many of the county’s farmworkers may feel worlds away from Silicon Valley, but the cost of living is still in line with the Bay Area. The annual per-capita income in San Mateo County is roughly $84,000, according to recent U.S. Census data, but the number dips to roughly $59,000 in Pescadero and significantly less than that for the region’s minimum wage workers. Housing costs alone quickly eat up earnings. Three-bedroom homes like the one rented by Gomez and his family are listed for $4,000 or more on sites such as Zillow. Then there’s everything else. “Right now, the money coming in just isn’t enough.” said Irma Flores, who should be retired but works caring for an elderly adult to help make ends meet. “Everything is so expensive.” Like many in the community, Flores relies on outside help to get by. She was among dozens of people – mostly mothers – lined up outside a Pescadero school to load up on groceries provided for free by ALAS, a local nonprofit that serves coastal farmworkers in Northern California. “We’re just really grateful to be able to provide culturally appropriate foods that we know our families are going to use in their kitchens,” said ALAS Farmworker and Essential Worker Program Director Sandra Sencion. Volunteers pack food into bags alongside the organization’s Farmworker Equity Express Bus, which travels the area providing free resources, from food and basic necessities to educational and mental health services. Some of the produce was purchased directly from Gavilanes Farm, the farm operated by Margarito Gomez. “It’s a very special bus,” Sencion said. “Really connecting with our community to be able to bring them the services that are really challenging to get for some of our farmworkers and essential workers.” For people like Flores, the program helps relieve some of that economic stress. “This helps us because every week they bring something different,” she said. “One week it’s food. Another week, it’s clothing, soap or other essentials.” Leydi Cervantes was also in line. She arrived in Pescadero nearly 32 years ago as a teenager and is now married with four children. “Both parents have to work and sometimes that’s still not enough,” said Cervantes, who earns a living packing lettuce. “So, one of them has to take a second job. My husband finishes work here, then goes to another job at a horse ranch.” Sometimes it’s still not enough. “When we just can’t make it, we apply for financial assistance programs that help us pay the rent,” she said. Like many farmworkers here, Cervantes rents her home and said she has given up hope of owning her own. According to Zillow, the average home price in Pescadero currently hovers north of $1 million. San Mateo County officials have identified a shortage of affordable housing in Pescadero and in neighboring Half Moon Bay, which now faces a lawsuit from the state for failing to comply with mandated housing plans. One of the proposed developments at the center of this battle is the 555 Kelly Avenue project, a landmark 40-unit affordable housing complex for elderly farmworkers. It was originally proposed in 2022 and propelled forward after the 2023 mass shooting in Half Moon Bay that exposed the substandard living conditions of local farmworkers. Despite the lack of affordable housing in the area, there’s been local opposition to the project from some residents and city leaders regarding density and traffic concerns. Following a successful local petition drive, the project’s fate now rests in the hands of voters on the upcoming November ballot. In the meantime, Cervantes and other farmworkers say they’ll keep pushing forward, leaning on the community for help when necessary. “Keep going,” Cervantes said. “Anything is possible. And don’t be ashamed to ask for help.”
headlines.source: Hilda Gutierrez, Michael Bott, Son Vo, Robbie Beasom and Jeremy Carroll

headlines.title: Many upset after community murals on East San Jose building painted over
headlines.description: Many were upset after two murals outside of a building sold about a year ago in East San Jose were painted over by the building’s new owner. A social media post by nonprofit ConXión says Martha’s Kitchen painted over two community murals on the outside of the building ConXión sold to them in 2025. “No warning, nothing else was painted, so it wasn’t like they were painting the whole building, it was just those things,” President and CEO of ConXión Lori Chávez said. “The murals themselves have a lot of significance because it shows history.” Chávez says one of the murals was created with young people who participated in an after-school program for native American and Latino students. “That mural was done by Jimmy Fonseca and it was done in collaboration with the youth, with kids at the after-school program,” Chávez said. Chávez says ConXión discussed the murals with Martha’s Kitchen during negotiations to sell the building. “We told them, we love these murals, they’re important to the community, we’d like for you to keep them, inside and out, and he agreed, ‘Yes they’re beautiful, we’ll keep them’,” Chávez said. But Martha’s Kitchen Executive Director Bill Lee says that conversation never happened. “They never raised the issue, and that’s one of the reasons I’m very disappointed with that social media post because they never asked us to preserve the mural,” Lee said. Lee says Martha’s Kitchen told ConXión in October that it intended to paint over the murals. He says the exterior needed to be painted, and the murals did not represent Martha’s Kitchen’s mission. “Unfortunately, the mural neither represents what our organization does, we feed people who are starving, we feed the homeless,” Lee said. Lee says Martha’s Kitchen plans to put a new mural on a nearby wall, one that he says will reflect the organization’s work. “That mural will represent food being grown, food being prepared, food being consumed which is what we do, we’re here for the community, we rescue food that would otherwise go into the landfill and feed people that would otherwise go hungry,” Lee said. ConXión says the murals represented an important part of the community’s story. Martha’s Kitchen says it plans to replace them with artwork that better reflects its mission. San Jose City Councilman Bien Doan sent a statement addressing the situation. “I was very disappointed to see the murals were covered up. I know Martha’s Kitchen wants to be a good neighbor, but that means respecting and embracing our cultural values and histories, especially with respect to our children. It is my hope that this mural will be replaced soon and that they incorporate imaging representative of our youth and indigenous residents,” he wrote.

headlines.title: 4 arrested in the East Bay after attempted robbery in San Mateo County
headlines.description: Four people were arrested in the East Bay in connection with an attempted robbery in San Mateo County Thursday, according to the Alameda County Sheriff’s Office. The sheriff’s office said at around 3:50 p.m., San Mateo police broadcasted a BOLO (Be On the Lookout) for a silver Audi associated with an attempted robbery. Police had attempted a traffic stop on the vehicle as it entered Alameda County after crossing the San Mateo Bridge, but the vehicle did not stop. With the use of plate reader technology, sheriff’s officials said the Audi was found, and the Alameda County Sheriff’s Office airplane (ALCO 2) confirmed the car’s location near Washington Avenue and Spring Lake Drive in San Leandro. ALCO 2, followed the vehicle to Grand Avenue and Lake Park in Oakland, where the suspects left the Audi and entered an awaiting black Mercedes, according to authorities. ALCO 2 tracked the Mercedes until sheriff’s deputies initiated a traffic stop on westbound I-580 near Powell Street in Emeryville, officials said. The sheriff’s office informed the Mercedes yielded and deputies conducted a “high-risk traffic stop.” That’s when the sheriff’s office said the four suspects were taken into custody. They added the circumstances surrounding the attempted robbery are being investigated by San Mateo police.

headlines.title: Crews respond to Rancho San Antonio Park fire in Cupertino
headlines.description: Emergency crews are responding to a brush fire Thursday afternoon at Rancho San Antonio Park in Cupertino. Aerial coverage from NBC Bay Area’s SkyRanger showed air tankers dropping retardant on the blaze. No other information was immediately available.

headlines.title: Major construction projects in the Bay Area to impact weekend traffic
headlines.description: Major construction projects are set for both sides of the Bay over the weekend; one will close all westbound lanes of the Carquinez Bridge and the other will limit lanes on one of the busiest stretches of Highway 101 in San Francisco. Starting Friday at 11 p.m., Caltrans will close two lanes in each direction of the Highway 101 Bayshore Freeway (Hospital Curve) area and expects to keep them closed until Monday morning. Caltrans is suggesting Interstate 280 or public transportation as an option as they shutter the lanes to work on the median near Hospital Curve. It’s part of a longer-term project that started in 2025. “So, what’s happening is on two of the fast lanes going northbound and two of the fast lanes going southbound between Cesar Chavez and 10th will be closed, but there will be two lanes that will remain open in both directions throughout the entire closure,” Lori Shepherd, with Caltrans said. Across the Bay, all westbound lanes of the Carquinez Bridge are set to shut down Friday night as well. “Westbound I-80 Carquinez Bridge, also known as the Alfred Zampa Memorial Bridge, we will be shutting down that span starting Friday night,” Sabrina Martinez with Caltrans Solano County said. It’s all part of a pavement rehab project. The westbound closure starts at 10 p.m. Friday and is scheduled to reopen by Monday at 3 a.m. Drivers are being pointed to I-680 as an alternate. Caltrans has been trying to get the word out. “We are hoping we deter motorists from coming this way and minimizing as much traffic impact as possible, hopefully will more prefer to take out detours,” Martinez said. The eastbound direction of the bridge will remain open. The San Francisco Bay Ferry said it would provide additional ferry trips Saturday and Sunday on the Vallejo route during the westbound closure.

headlines.title: Motorcyclist killed in collision on El Camino Real in Palo Alto
headlines.description: A man was killed in Palo Alto on Wednesday after the motorcycle he was driving collided with a car, police said. On Wednesday just before 4:30 p.m., officers were called to the 100 block of El Camino Real on a report of a collision. A man in his 20s was ejected from his motorcycle and was taken to a hospital, where he died, according to Palo Alto police. Investigators believe that the motorcycle was traveling south when it collided with a sedan that was going northbound and making a left turn into a business. The exact cause of the crash remains under investigation. The driver of the sedan, a woman in her 20s, remained at the scene and cooperated with police, the department said. Anyone with information helpful to this investigation is asked to call the Palo Alto Police Department 24-hour dispatch center at 650-329-2413. Anonymous tips can be sent via text message by texting the keyword PAPD and the tip to 847411.

headlines.title: 2-year-old girl dies after suspected Richmond arson, bringing death toll to 3
headlines.description: A 2-year-old girl who was critically injured in a Richmond house fire allegedly set by her uncle has died, police said Thursday. Suspect Sergio Rivera-Vega was arrested on suspicion of starting the blaze Tuesday night at the home located along the 200 block of 15th Street, according to police. The fire killed Rivera-Vega’s 47-year-old father and 5-year-old nephew and left his 33-year-old sister – mother of the two children – in critical condition. “The mom who is fighting for her life right now, I don’t know if she knows that she doesn’t have children anymore,” Richmond police Lt. Joseph England said. Rivera-Vega lived in the house. Police officials said a motive for the alleged arson is still under investigation. “Our investigators, their number one goal is to figure out why this happened, why this person would do this to their family,” England said. “That is what everybody wants to know.” The blaze happened just two doors down from another alleged, but completely unrelated, arson fire. Richmond Fire Department crews were sent to the first fire at about 8:15 p.m. Tuesday. After that fire was under control at about 8:45 p.m., bystanders alerted firefighters of another fire at a nearby home, which is the one Rivera-Vega allegedly started, according to authorities. The second fire was under control by about 9:25 p.m., according to Richmond Fire Chief Aaron Osorio. Three of the victims were taken to the hospital, where the children died. The suspect’s father died at the scene. All of the victims were injured or killed by the fire, and there is no evidence that they were shot or stabbed prior to the alleged arson, according to police. Court records appear to show a family member took a restraining order out on Rivera-Vega in 2022 but dropped it later that year. Investigators confirmed they have had prior contact with him. “We are not going to comment in regards to what the prior contacts were,” England said. “This is all being investigated by the detectives right now.” No injuries or deaths related to the first fire were reported, but police did arrest a suspect in that case. Their name wasn’t immediately released.
headlines.source: NBC Bay Area staff and Bay City News

headlines.title: Police investigate reported stabbing at Oakland's Castlemont High School
headlines.description: Police on Thursday were investigating a reported stabbing at Castlemont High School in Oakland. The incident was reported around 10:15 a.m. School officials said several people got into a fight in a back parking lot. A victim, described by police as a juvenile, was taken to a hospital after being “injured by a bladed object.” The Oakland Unified School District said the victim’s injury was non-life threatening. “We are working closely with their family to ensure they have what they need,” OUSD said in a statement. “Everyone who was impacted by this incident is being supported by school and district staff.” Multiple juveniles were detained in connection with the incident, according to police. No other information was immediately available.

headlines.title: FBI seizes devices from ex-Rep. Eric Swalwell and searches his D.C. home
headlines.description: Federal agents seized electronic devices from former Rep. Eric Swalwell and searched his Washington, D.C., home as part of an investigation into allegations of sexual misconduct by the ex-Democratic congressman from California, according to The Associated Press and NBC News. Swalwell was stopped by the FBI at the San Francisco airport on Saturday and his electronic devices were taken as part of the execution of a search warrant, a person familiar with the matter told NBC News. Agents executed a search warrant at his home a day later, said the person, who was not authorized to publicly discuss an ongoing investigation and spoke on the condition of anonymity. An attorney for Swalwell did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Swalwell has previously denied allegations of sexual assault and misconduct. The FBI declined to comment on the warrants. Swalwell announced his resignation from Congress in April following allegations that he had sexually assaulted a woman twice, including when she worked for him. The San Francisco Chronicle, followed by CNN, first reported the allegations. CNN also reported that three other women alleged various kinds of sexual misconduct by Swalwell, including sending them unsolicited explicit messages or nude photos. The seven-term lawmaker had been seen as one of the leading candidates in California’s gubernatorial race before dropping out after the allegations surfaced. The office of Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg confirmed in April that it was investigating Swalwell after a former staffer told CNN and the Chronicle that Swalwell raped her at a hotel while he was in New York City for a charity gala in 2024. In a statement, Bragg’s office encouraged “survivors and anyone with knowledge of these allegations to contact our Special Victims Division.” Swalwell, an Iowa native, was elected in 2012 and represented a House district east of San Francisco. He launched a presidential run in April 2019 but ended it a few months later after failing to catch on with voters. He was one of Republican President Donald Trump’s top Democratic antagonists in Congress. He was a prominent member of the House Judiciary and Intelligence committees during Trump’s first term and served as one of several Democratic prosecutors for Trump’s second impeachment after the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol. Swalwell was removed from the Intelligence Committee by then-House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif., in 2023 based on Swalwell’s contact with a suspected Chinese spy, Christine Fang. Fang was reported to have come into contact with Swalwell’s campaign as he was first running for Congress in 2012 and to have participated in fundraising for his 2014 campaign. Federal investigators alerted Swalwell to their concerns and briefed Congress about Fang in 2015, at which point Swalwell says he cut off contact with her. He was not accused of wrongdoing and a House Ethics Committee investigation that was opened in 2021 closed two years later without any action. ____ Associated Press reporter Michael R. Sisak in New York contributed to this report.
headlines.source: Alanna Durkin Richer | The Associated Press and NBC News

headlines.title: New effort to save National Archives sites in 3 U.S. cities, including San Bruno
headlines.description: Tens of thousands of historical records that tell the story of the United States, including immigration records, may no longer be available to the public. The Trump administration recently announced plans for the National Archives in Chicago, Seattle and San Bruno to be shuttered for good. Bay Area Congressman Kevin Mullin and others in Congress are fighting that closure. “We need to do whatever we can to protect them and have the expertise here properly employed to continue to protect these records,” Mullin said from the National Archives building in San Bruno. Inside the building is 1 million cubic feet of historical records and 100,000 permanent records that are open to the public, by appointment. The documents are more than 100 years old, like Native American boarding school records, Chinese immigration papers from the Exclusion Act era and pages from the Alcatraz warden’s notebook. “The historical value of these documents, they are not meant to be digitized or transported anywhere,” Mullin said. “These have to be preserved here.” To do that, Mullin and Rep. Judy Chu are co-leading and sending a letter to the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), stating the closures are a mistake and urging reconsideration. So far, nearly 40 members of Congress have signed on to save the archives. The letter questions what the government’s plans are to move the materials, where they’re going and whether the “required administrative procedure was followed in making this decision.” An email sent to employees by National Archives COO Jay Trainer in June said the closures would “reduce costs” and “reduce estate portfolio.” Nothing was said about what will happen to the full-time employees at the archives. The archives in San Bruno have been life-changing for many people looking for answers about their family’s past. “For the longest time, I didn’t know I was a descendant of Wong Kim Ark,” Sandra Wong said. “After I did the research with Wong Kim Ark, I got a copy of my father’s file…I’d ever seen a photo of him as a young boy. That was the first time that I saw that.” Born and raised in San Francisco’s Chinatown, Wong Kim Ark cemented birthright citizenship in the U.S. more than a century ago. In July, the Supreme Court upheld his win for birthright citizenship. Wong said, without NARA, she would not know what she knows today about her family. Leona Lau has a similar story. She found her great-grandfather’s 134-year-old Hawaiian naturalization certificate in the archives. “I sent a request to NARA San Bruno…the archivist, he emailed me back and says, ‘I found him,'” Lau said. “That milestone set my family on a path to U.S. citizenship…I do now realize I’m the first generation born here in the U.S.” Lau and Wong are joining the nonprofit Save Our National Archives (SONA) to fight the potential closures. Once SONA heard the news, it immediately started organizing. “We have a letter writing campaign where we’ve had hundreds of people write personal letters to the acting archivists of the National Archives and also sending copies to their local Congress people,” SONA member Grant Din said. “We did an online petition, which has almost 7,000 signatures already.” There are 13 total National Archives across the U.S. California has two of them – the one in San Bruno and another in Riverside. Moving forward, Mullin said he is working on legislation that would protect the national facilities by requiring congressional approval before any closure. Mullin will hold a news conference on Monday to discuss the legislation and efforts he’s helping to lead to keep the archives open.
headlines.source: Christine Ni, Janelle Wang and Alex Bozovic
